articles.title: Jeff Bezos gave Eva Longoria and Bill McRaven $100 million, but she challenges the belief that giving back requires wealth, saying ‘impact doesn’t come from how much money you have’
articles.summary: Philanthropy is often associated with people who have fortunes large enough to fund schools, charities and ambitious social programmes.
articles.body: Philanthropy is often associated with people who have fortunes large enough to fund schools, charities and ambitious social programmes. Yet the ability to support others does not necessarily depend on the size of a bank account. As reported by Fortune, actress Eva Longoria has been making that distinction after receiving a $50 million philanthropic award from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, alongside retired US Navy admiral Bill McRaven. Two years after the recognition, Longoria says the experience has changed how she approaches charitable work, but she also wants to challenge the idea that meaningful contributions are reserved for wealthy individuals.How Jeff Bezos brought Eva Longoria and Bill McRaven togetherIn 2024, Eva Longoria and retired admiral Bill McRaven were selected as recipients of the Bezos Courage and Civility Award, an initiative established by Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos to recognise people working to improve society.“The Courage and Civility Award makes it possible for us at the Eva Longoria Foundation to create long-term impact with transformative giving.”Each recipient received $50 million, bringing the combined philanthropic commitment to $100 million. The funding was intended to support causes that reflected their respective areas of work.For Longoria, the award offered an opportunity to expand programmes focused on education, economic opportunities and support for Latino communities in the United States. McRaven, meanwhile, had plans to direct his share towards education and support services for military personnel and their families.McRaven is widely recognised for overseeing the 2011 US military operation that resulted in the death of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden.Why Eva Longoria believes giving back is about more than moneyLongoria's experience with the award has given her a larger platform to discuss charitable giving, but her message is not centred on financial donations. In an interview with Fortune, she said, “This award has allowed me to continue investing those resources into the communities and causes I care deeply about—supporting Latina entrepreneurs, expanding access to education, and backing organizations that are driving real change on the ground.”Her understanding of giving back includes mentoring, sharing professional knowledge and helping small businesses find opportunities they might otherwise struggle to access.What Longoria has done with her philanthropic awardLongoria's involvement in charitable work began well before she received recognition from Bezos. In 2012, she established the Eva Longoria Foundation, which focuses on improving educational and entrepreneurial opportunities for Latinas in the United States. Its work includes helping women access resources that can support their education and participation in business. She also founded Eva's Heroes, an organisation that supports young adults with intellectual special needs.The $50 million award has provided additional resources for these efforts. Longoria has described the funding as an opportunity to plan longer-term programmes and direct investment towards communities and organisations working on the ground.Her charitable activities also sit alongside a varied business career. The former Desperate Housewives actress has developed interests in entertainment, entrepreneurship and sports, including her luxury tequila brand Casa Del Sol, production company Hyphenate Media Group and investment in women's football club Angel City FC.She has also been associated with an early investment in the John Wick film franchise. These business activities have helped establish her as more than an actor, while her foundation work has remained a separate part of her public life. Longoria has said,“Receiving that support was incredibly meaningful, not just because of the scale of the gift, but because it represented trust and responsibility.”What Bill McRaven plans to do with his $50 millionThe other half of the $100 million commitment went to Bill McRaven, whose philanthropic priorities reflect his military background. McRaven has said he intends to support educational programmes for future military leaders and children of deceased veterans. Mental health assistance for serving military personnel is another area included in his plans.A former four-star admiral, McRaven held senior leadership positions in the US military and later served as chancellor of the University of Texas System. His work has included military education, leadership development and public service.The Bezos Courage and Civility Award has previously recognised other prominent figures involved in humanitarian and social initiatives. Among its recipients are civil rights advocate Van Jones, chef and humanitarian José Andrés, and singer Dolly Parton.Growing debate over billionaire philanthropy and public responsibilityLarge charitable donations attract attention because they can finance projects that would be difficult for smaller organisations to undertake. But the concentration of philanthropic resources among a relatively small number of wealthy individuals has also raised questions about how much responsibility should rest with them. The Giving Pledge is one example of an effort to encourage large-scale charitable commitments. Established in 2010 by Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates and Warren Buffett, it invites billionaires to commit at least half of their wealth to charitable causes during their lifetimes or through their wills.More than 250 individuals and families have signed the pledge since its launch. However, making a commitment and distributing the promised wealth are not the same thing. For Liz Baker, chief executive of Greater Good Charities, waiting for wealthy donors to address community problems leaves too much work undone. The organisation she leads has distributed more than $1 billion in support across 121 countries since 2006. Speaking to Fortune, Baker argued that charitable participation should not be limited to people capable of making substantial financial contributions.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: In a generous move, Tyreek Hill's family foundation contributes $40,000 to Coffee High and Atkinson County High's athletic programs, empowering youth sports in Georgia. Discover the details of the donation and its impact.
articles.body: Tyreek Hill was born in Pearson, Georgia and attended Coffee High School in Douglas, about a 20-minute drive away, according to WALB and the O’Colly. His family foundation presented a $40,000 check to the athletic department at Coffee High and Atkinson County High, as a post on the foundation’s website states. The Tyreek Hill Family Foundation announced the $40,000 donation on May 25, 2023. Athlon Sports revisited it in a report published on October 30, 2026 and Yahoo Sports carried a version of that piece.Hill moved from Pearson to Coffee County for high school According to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Hill was brought up in Pearson, Atkinson County, but went on to study at Coffee High from the time he was in the ninth grade. Hill told the paper that his grandparents felt he needed a change. O'Colly, Oklahoma State University’s student newspaper, described Atkinson County High as small and said his family chose Coffee High, known for its sports programmes and exposure. He studied there in football and track, then attended Junior College for two years.The $40,000 check was presented during a free youth football camp in DouglasHill, at that time, Miami Dolphins wide receiver, concluded a full-house camp on Sunday, May 21, 2023, with children of Coffee, Atkinson and Irwin counties being invited, Daily Coffee Press reported. The foundation post mentions a $40,000 check to support the athletic programmes at Coffee High School and Atkinson County High School.Separately, a photo shared by Daily Coffee Press shows Hill presenting a check to Atkinson County, which was accepted by the principal and assistant principal of Atkinson County Middle School. However, the available posts do not clarify whether this was a separate donation or part of the previously reported $40,000 contribution. The foundation describes its mission as empowering children.The foundation has kept giving in Georgia since the campAccording to Every.org, the foundation is a youth development charity organisation which operates from Pearson and received nonprofit status in 2017. The foundation's first gala, in December 2021, raised over $177,000 for youth mental health programmes, according to its website. In October 2024, Hill’s foundation launched a Hurricane Helene relief campaign for Georgia and matched donations up to $20,000, Fox 5 Atlanta reported. It also provides Cheetah Scholars, a college scholarship program giving out 10 scholarships each year and increasing by $5,000 to the scholarship fund for every touchdown scored by Hill in the 2024-25 season.High school sports participation reached 8,266,244 students in 2024-25Hill’s gift went to the school athletic department at a time when families are spending more to play. The Aspen Institute’s State of Play 2025 report found that the average family spent $1016 on a child’s primary sport in 2024, 46% more than in 2019. articles.title: ‘Blue Tsunami’ to ‘Dem-olition’: How the world covered US midterm election results
articles.summary: Democrats have swept to power in both chambers of the US Congress, delivering a crushing midterm blow to President Donald Trump and leaving Republicans
articles.body: Democrats have swept to power in both chambers of the US Congress, delivering a crushing midterm blow to President Donald Trump and leaving Republicans facing a political reckoning halfway through his second term. The party scored historic victories in traditionally Republican strongholds, flipped key seats across the country and registered a series of firsts, including the election of the first Muslim senator and the first openly gay man to the Senate. The results have not only disrupted Trump's legislative agenda but also raised questions about the future of the MAGA movement and the road to 2028 Presidential elections.From a “Blue Tsunami” to a “Dem-olition” job, newspapers across the world found their own ways to capture the scale of the Republican rout. While some focused on the domestic political fallout and the growing cracks within Trump's camp, others highlighted the role of the Iran war and economic discontent in the Democratic sweep.Here's how the world reacted: The Times of India‘Trump loses the war at home’The Times of India described the outcome as a political defeat for Trump, with the headline declaring that Democrats had stormed Republican strongholds, seized both chambers of Congress and won a majority of governorships.The Economic Times‘Trump & Team Beaten Blue’The Economic Times captured the scale of the Republican setback with a play on the colour associated with the Democratic Party. Its coverage highlighted how Trump's tariff policies and belligerence had come back to haunt his party, while examining the implications of the results for global markets and India's economic interests. South China Morning Post, Hong Kong‘Blue Tsunami Sweeps the US’The South China Morning Post went with a image of celebrating Democratic supporters and the headline “Blue Tsunami Sweeps the US”. Its subheading described the outcome as a disastrous night for Trump, with Democrats taking the House and Senate and leaving global leaders to reassess their strategies. Financial Times, UK‘Crushing midterm rebuke to Trump’The Financial Times called the results a crushing electoral rebuke to Trump. Its supporting headlines highlighted the role of the cost-of-living crisis in driving the Democratic wave, with voters sweeping Republicans out of power in Congress. It also pointed to the political blame game beginning within the Republican Party, with JD Vance pinning responsibility on the Iran war, alongside movements in oil prices and technology stocks. Le Journal de Montréal, Canada‘Toute une claque’ (Quite a slap)The French-language Canadian daily went for a short, punchy headline that needed little explanation. “Toute une claque” captured the scale of the setback for Trump. Chicago Sun-Times, US‘Dem-olition’The Chicago Sun-Times brought wordplay to the front page with “Dem-olition”, combining the Democratic Party's name with the idea of a political demolition job. The cover featured Juliana Stratton celebrating with supporters after her Senate victory, placing a local electoral triumph within the broader national blue wave. El Mundo, Spain‘Trump blames the war for the electoral tsunami that sweeps away Republicans’Spanish newspaper El Mundo focused on Trump's response to the defeat, particularly his attempt to attribute the Republican losses to the war with Iran. Its front page featured the president against the backdrop of the US flag, with the headline highlighting how the conflict had become a factor in the electoral backlash. Tehran Times, Iran‘US Hegemony Crumbling; Iran Will Never Surrender’The Iranian newspaper described the result as an outcome fo the conflict between Washington and Tehran. The English-language daily, which is closely aligned with the Iranian government, portrayed the Democratic victory as a sign of declining American influence, with the headline “US Hegemony Crumbling; Iran Will Never Surrender”. Daily Mail, UK‘MAGA Turns on Trump’The Daily Mail led with the headline: “MAGA Turns on Trump”, which was accompanied by a report highlighting how JD Vance and even Donald Trump Jr were blaming the president's handling of the Iran war for the Republican wipeout. The Guardian, UK‘Trumped’The Guardian chose a play on the president's name for its front page, with “Trumped” appearing in large yellow lettering beneath a photograph of jubilant Democratic supporters. Its accompanying description noted that the president's party had been stripped of control of Congress. New York Post, US‘Blue Tsunami’The New York Post described the Democratic victory as a "Blue Tsunami". Its front page featured an illustration inspired by Japanese artist Hokusai's famous Great Wave, with Trump appearing to be swept away by a gigantic blue wave. The Australian, Australia‘The Donald Deflation’The Australian opted for a pun, declaring “The Donald Deflation” as Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress. Its coverage connected the Republican defeat to inflation, fuel prices and the Iran war, while examining the political damage to Trump's MAGA movement. The Washington Post, US‘Voters swing to Democrats’The Washington Post took a direct approach, with the headline “Voters swing to Democrats” summarising the electoral shift. Its subheading said the party was poised to take power on Capitol Hill with an eagerness to thwart Trump's agenda. The Wall Street Journal, US‘Democrats Score Big Wins’The Wall Street Journal highlighted the historic victories in deep-red states, noting how the Democrats had flipped key seats and put control of the House beyond Republican reach. Its front page featured images of victorious candidates and celebrations across the country.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: How to grow a bay leaf tree in a pot at home: Simple tips to enjoy fresh tej patta for your everyday curries
articles.summary: Drop a tej patta into hot oil, and the whole kitchen smells like dal, pulao or biryani is on its way.
articles.body: Drop a tej patta into hot oil, and the whole kitchen smells like dal, pulao or biryani is on its way. Most of us buy those leaves in a packet, and by the time they reach the kitchen, they’ve lost some of their punch. Growing your own is a lovely alternative, and it’s easier than you might expect. Tej patta comes from a sturdy, glossy evergreen tree that can live happily in a large pot on a sunny balcony or terrace. It does grow slowly, so patience is part of the deal, but the reward is a plant that gives you fresh, fragrant leaves for years. Here’s how to start.Start with the right plantFirst, a little botany. Tej patta is Cinnamomum tamala, also called Indian bay leaf. It’s different from the Mediterranean bay laurel used in Western cooking. Its leaves are longer and wider, olive green, with three veins running down the length. The easiest way to begin is with a young sapling from a reputable nursery. You can also grow it from a cutting or air layering, but it takes patience, and seeds can take six to eight weeks to sprout and a year or more to grow into a small plant.Pick a big pot and good soilBecause it’s a tree, tej patta needs room, so choose a medium to large pot with plenty of drainage holes. Fill it with a fertile, well-draining mix, such as garden soil with compost and a little sand or coco peat, so the roots never sit in water. A slightly acidic to neutral soil is fine. Plant the sapling at the same depth it was growing at in the nursery pot, and keep it in indirect light for a few days while it settles in.Give it sun, and water with careTej patta loves warmth and does best with about four to six hours of sunlight a day, which also gives the leaves a stronger flavour. Keep it in a sunny balcony or terrace spot, but give it some shade in the harshest afternoon heat. For watering, wait until the top inch or two of the soil feels dry, then water thoroughly. Don’t let it dry out completely, and don’t leave it standing in water. You’ll need less water in the monsoon and winter.Feed, prune and repot when neededSince it’s slow-growing, tej patta doesn’t need a lot of fuss. Feed it compost or a balanced fertiliser every four to six weeks during the growing season. Prune lightly once a year, or when it outgrows its space, to keep it bushy and manageable. Every two to three years, or when roots start poking out of the drainage holes, move it to a pot one size bigger. It doesn’t like frost, so in cold regions, bring it indoors for winter.Harvest slowly, and use it wellBe patient with this one. Wait until the plant is well established and has plenty of healthy leaves before you start picking, then take just a few mature leaves at a time so that it can keep growing. Use them fresh, or dry them in the shade for a few days to intensify the aroma. Drop one into your dal, pulao, biryani or curry. And remember that the leaf is meant to flavour the dish, so take it out before eating.Disclaimer:This article is intended for general informational purposes only. Buy your plant from a reputable nursery and confirm that it is actually Indian bay leaf (Cinnamomum tamala) before cooking with it, since some other laurel-type plants are toxic. Growth rate and results vary with climate, pot size and care, so consult a local nursery for advice suited to your area.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: How to save your balcony plants from extreme pollution and smog
articles.summary: The air has turned toxic. You can smell it, feel it, and it’s making you sick. Now, imagine your plants outside — in your garden or on your balcony.
articles.body: The air has turned toxic. You can smell it, feel it, and it’s making you sick. Now, imagine your plants outside — in your garden or on your balcony. They need far more than regular watering. From washing dust off leaves to creating natural barriers, here are a few simple changes that can help plants survive the season of pollution.From glossy to dullThe leaves that were once glossy and green begin to look dull. A fine grey film settles over the foliage. Flowering plants stop producing buds and even hardy varieties seem to lose their vitality.During periods of severe air pollution and smog, balcony plants are exposed to much more than ordinary dust. Particulate matter, including PM2.5 and PM10, settles on leaves, clogs their surfaces and can interfere with the natural processes through which plants exchange gases and make food.Unlike indoor plants, balcony gardens have little protection from the elements. They are exposed to traffic emissions, construction dust, industrial pollutants and changing weather conditions, often for several hours every day. While plants can tolerate a certain amount of environmental stress, prolonged exposure to high pollution levels can affect their growth, damage foliage and make them more vulnerable to pests and disease.It needs a little seasonal care, some protection from direct exposure and a change in the way you approach watering, cleaning and maintenance.Give leaves a regular clean-upClean leaves regularly. Fine particulate matter settles on leaf surfaces, forming a layer of dust that can interfere with light absorption and normal gas exchange. This is particularly noticeable on broad-leaved plants such as monstera, rubber plants, peace lilies and hibiscus.Use a gentle spray of clean water to wash the foliage, preferably in the morning when there is enough time for the leaves to dry. For plants with large, sturdy leaves, wipe the surface gently with a damp, soft cloth, taking care to clean both sides. Smaller plants can be rinsed with a light shower using a watering can or spray nozzle.Avoid using soap, detergent, milk or homemade chemical mixtures to clean leaves. During particularly bad pollution spells, inspect your plants every two or three days and clean them as needed. There is no need to wash them daily, especially if the weather is cold or humid, as persistently wet foliage can encourage fungal problems.Create a protective green barrierArrange plants in layers, with sturdier plants positioned along the outer edge and more delicate varieties placed behind them. Dense foliage can intercept some larger dust particles and reduce direct exposure to windblown debris.Plants such as areca palm, bamboo palm, ficus, spider plant and certain varieties of dracaena can be used to create a layered green screen, depending on the amount of sunlight and space available. Tall planters, trellises and compact shrubs can also help shield smaller flowering plants from direct exposure.If your balcony faces a busy road or construction site, consider installing a breathable outdoor mesh screen. It can help reduce the amount of larger dust entering the space. Avoid completely sealing the balcony with plastic sheets or non-breathable coverings, as this can restrict ventilation, trap humidity and create conditions favourable to fungal growth.Water wisely, but do not overwaterPollution stress can make plants look dehydrated, but that does not necessarily mean they need more water. During winter, when temperatures are lower and sunlight is weaker, soil takes longer to dry. Overwatering can lead to root rot, yellowing leaves and fungal infections, adding to the stress plants are already experiencing.Check the top inch of soil before watering. If it feels dry, water the plant; if it is still moist, wait another day. Water at the base rather than splashing foliage unnecessarily, particularly during damp or foggy weather.It is also important to ensure that pots have adequate drainage. Remove standing water from trays and avoid allowing roots to remain submerged. If the air is particularly dry, grouping plants together can help create a slightly more humid microclimate, but do not overcrowd them.Give plants a break from fertilisers and pruningPollution season is not the best time to push plants into vigorous growth. When plants are already dealing with environmental stress, excessive fertilising can do more harm than good.Remove dead, damaged or badly discoloured leaves using clean pruning scissors. This helps prevent the spread of disease and allows the plant to direct its energy towards healthy growth. However, avoid aggressive pruning during periods of stress. A plant that has lost some foliage needs time to recover rather than additional disturbance.Keep an eye out for pests as well. Weak or stressed plants can become more susceptible to infestations.Know when to bring plants indoorsIf pollution levels remain extremely high for several days, consider temporarily moving smaller and more sensitive plants indoors. Place them near a bright window where they receive adequate indirect light. Avoid positioning them directly beside heaters, air-conditioners or cold draughts.You can also use a simple transparent plant cover or a small portable greenhouse for particularly delicate plants, provided there is sufficient ventilation and the temperature does not rise excessively. Remember to uncover plants periodically and check for condensation.Choose resilient plants for the next seasonIf your balcony garden is repeatedly affected by pollution, it may be worth rethinking your plant selection. Hardy varieties that tolerate changing weather conditions and occasional dust exposure are generally easier to maintain.Consider areca palms, snake plants, money plants, rubber plants, spider plants and bougainvillea, depending on your balcony's sunlight and climate. No plant is immune to pollution, but these varieties are generally adaptable and relatively forgiving.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) on Thursday said he was in support of President Trump’s recently announced plan to stop aid to Israel.

“I agree with him on that,” El-Sayed said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

“I don’t think that we should be continuing to subsidize a foreign military that has done the worst things with our money. I agree. I’d love to work with him on doing that. In fact, I don’t know that we should be continuing to sell weapons to a country that is, again, using our weapons to do awful things,” the senator-elect added.

On Tuesday, Trump said that he had come to a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to stop aid to Israel this year.

In an interview with Fox News’s “Fox & Friends,” the president said he and the Israeli leader made a deal “months ago” for the U.S. to halt its aid to Israel.

“They’re fine with it,” Trump said. “They’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore.”

Trump said Washington would continue to assist Israel if they needed it and that the country had been “a great ally.”

The end of aid would mark a key shift in American foreign policy. Israel is seen as one of the biggest recipients of foreign aid from the U.S., with that aid requiring congressional authorization.

El-Sayed, who won his race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Tuesday, had advocated for halting aid to Israel and spending that money on domestic issues on the campaign trail.

American support for Israel has become a contentious issue in the last few years as Israel has carried out its war in Gaza, killing tens of thousands of Palestinians. Some have labeled Israel’s actions in the conflict a “genocide.”

articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) warned that Democrats would not let Vice President Vance off the hook for his record of supporting the Iran war after President Trump’s second-in-command said the conflict cost the GOP in the midterms.

Jeffries told Punchbowl News on Wednesday that Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio “have been consistent cheerleaders” for the war, which has now lasted more than eight months.

“Their record on standing behind Donald Trump and wasting billions of taxpayer dollars to drop bombs in Iran, and then, as a result of their actions, skyrocketing prices on the American people, particularly as it relates to gas, is one that certainly played a role in the decisive defeat that the MAGA extremists experienced,” the New York Democrat said.

“We’re not going to let JD Vance run away from his own record of supporting Donald Trump’s reckless and failed war,” he added.

Following his party’s defeat in Tuesday’s elections, Vance put it plainly in a lengthy social media post : “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

“But everyone knows why we lost,” the vice president continued. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Despite the rhetoric, as Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) pointed out , Vance was an early defender of the war. Ahead of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes that began the conflict on Feb. 28, he told The Washington Post there was “no chance” this would lead to a longer war in the Middle East.

He has also stood by Trump as he continues to threaten military operations against Iran, telling reporters in September that he “wouldn’t call it a war” despite an eruption of back-and-forth strikes in the region.

Exit polling indicated that economic frustrations were a key motivator for many midterm voters. Democrats flipped control of both chambers of Congress.

A recent survey from The Associated Press found that voters across the country blamed Trump’s tariffs and the Middle East conflict for rising costs. A CBS News exit poll also found that 75 percent of voters shared a negative view of the U.S. economy around Election Day.

articles.title: Xi’s not interested in a trilateral with Trump and Putin
articles.summary: The Chinese leader needs the world to focus on his shaky narrative of success.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, the Financial Times reported that Chinese, Russian and American officials are discussing a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, which is scheduled to start on Nov. 18.

The possibility of such a meeting in China, including Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and President Trump, has raised the specter of a modern-day Yalta Conference , the disastrous February 1945 gathering of Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin. That conference led to the Soviet absorption of Eastern Europe.

Many are now concerned that Xi, Putin and Trump will divide up Ukraine behind the backs of its leaders and people. Some analysts are speaking of a “ bad Yalta ” in Shenzhen.

It does not have to turn out that way, of course.

“The good news is that the leaders of the three most powerful nations will sit down to discuss the most pressing issues in our very troubled world,” Blaine Holt, a retired U.S. Air Force general who served as America’s deputy military representative to NATO, told me this month.

Dmitry Peskov, Putin’s spokesperson, told the Financial Times that “work is under way” to organize a trilateral, and China’s foreign ministry said it was “in communication with relevant parties regarding the meeting between the heads of state of China, Russia and the US.”

Moscow would clearly benefit from a three-way meeting.

“Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia,” wrote Eva Seiwert in the Diplomat.

Trump appears to like the idea of a grand gathering, as he has been pushing both Beijing and Moscow to participate in talks to reduce nuclear weapons and has long wanted to broker a peace in the Russia-Ukraine war. Trump did not rule out a discussion about the conflict in China.

But despite the foreign ministry’s statement, the Chinese are the least enthusiastic about a trilateral. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, after meeting Xi in Beijing on Oct. 30, said the Chinese leader had no interest in hosting a Ukraine-focused summit with Russia and the U.S.

“From his perspective, there is absolutely no preparation under way for a Ukraine summit involving the U.S., Russia and China,” Steinmeier told German public broadcaster ARD.

Xi apparently wants to avoid talking about the faraway war, taking the view that Ukraine has nothing to do with China. “He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict in which Europeans would also have to be at the negotiating table,” Steinmeier said .

Yes, it’s a European conflict, but China is a direct participant. After all, Beijing has been financing Russia’s war . It has continuously provided diplomatic and propaganda support to Moscow, and it has been supplying weapons components to Putin. China has allowed its citizens to travel to fight as mercenaries for Russia. There are People’s Liberation Army officers in Russia, and Beijing has been training Russian soldiers on Chinese soil.

In any event, the Chinese have made it clear where they stand. In July 2025, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas that Beijing does not want to see Russia lose in Ukraine because then the U.S. would be able to focus on China in East Asia. China, by implication, believes that the battle for the future of the world is now being fought on European soil.

As Andrew Michta of the Atlantic Council told me, and as China evidently believes, it is not possible to disaggregate Asia and Europe, which after all, are part of the same land mass. Similarly, Taiwanese believe that the fate of their island republic is being determined on the battlefields of Eastern Europe.

In any event, Xi, once in a private room with Putin and Trump, will almost certainly not be able to control the conversation.

“We hear Xi Jinping say any mention of the Ukraine war is off the table,” Holt noted. “But what happens when the door closes and it’s just the three of them and their interpreters? Pragmatism will take over when these essential discussions begin.”

Xi has a lot of reasons to be unhappy about Putin and Trump hijacking the Shenzhen meeting.

“A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation and cooperation,” wrote Seiwert.

The Chinese leader needs the world to focus on his shaky narrative of success, especially now when there are clear signs of a downturn in the country’s economy and the evident fraying of social cohesion throughout China. He does not need anyone undermining his propaganda narratives by talking about something else.
